title: Spacewar!, one of the first video games, drew its 1962 sky from real star charts

cover.alt: A round, dark computer screen in a wooden-looking cabinet shows two small glowing ships with green trails near a central dot of light.

body: In 1962 Steve Russell and friends at MIT wrote **Spacewar!** for the university's new DEC PDP-1 computer. Two players fly ships called the needle and the wedge around a star whose gravity pulls on both; the ships keep drifting when they stop thrusting, so a favourite tactic is to slingshot round the star. Peter Samson added a slowly scrolling backdrop drawn from real star charts, called the *Expensive Planetarium* after the PDP-1's high price. The code was public domain and spread to many of the few dozen PDP-1s.

slides.alt: Two glowing ships leave green trails as they swing around a bright central star on a round screen, with dim background stars appearing and fading.
slides.caption: A restored PDP-1 computer at the Computer History Museum runs Spacewar!: two ships swing around the central star, trailing green streaks, against a field of stars.

slides.label: roughly what a PDP-1 cost in 1962
slides.text: Only 53 were ever sold, most of them without a screen, so the original game reached only a narrow, academic audience.

items: A star whose gravity pulls on both ships

slides.heading: Spacewar!'s long shadow
slides.note: Galaxy Game and Computer Space (1971) and Asteroids were directly inspired by it

slides.prompt: Technicians at DEC, the PDP-1’s maker, reportedly ran Spacewar! on new machines before shipping them. Why?
slides.answer: It exercised every part of the hardware
slides.detail: So the story goes, second-hand: it was the only program around that tested the whole machine at once.

slides.question: What was the 'Expensive Planetarium'?
options: A star map drawn from real charts
A pricier model of the PDP-1
slides.explanation: Peter Samson's backdrop scrolled through real stars, shown at their relative brightness. The name poked fun at the PDP-1's price.
